## Execution Strategy

If the issue references a plan file with multiple tasks:

2. Each task: failing test → implement → verify → commit
3. After all tasks: run the verification below; only edit files and run verification, then the host commits and publishes after the run

## Test Integrity

Make failing tests pass by changing source code. Do not remove asserts, add skip or xfail, change expected values, or delete tests unless the issue declares the behavior change. If a test is wrong, say so under **Behavior changes** in the PR body with the reason.

Every existing test function you edit gets a **Behavior changes** line naming its pytest node id and the reason — even when the issue itself asks for the change. The merge's held-out gate runs the base copy of each test against your src and fails the merge on any failure no such line names; the issue asking for it does not count. Write one line per test, the node id relative to the project directory, as pytest prints it:

```
- tests/test_example.py::test_name — why the old expectation no longer holds
- tests/test_example.py::TestGroup::test_case — why
```

A parametrized test's line may name the test or each failing case (`tests/test_example.py::test_name[case]`). Tests you only add need no line.

## Autonomous Adaptations

Since no human is present:
- Treat the issue description and plan file as the approved spec.
- If the issue is genuinely too vague to implement, end your final message with `KEW_NEEDS_HUMAN: <reason>` and STOP.



## Token Budget

MEDIUM issue (~60k tokens/task). Scope: 2-4 files.

The #1 cause of autonomous failure is context exhaustion.
When in doubt, make tasks SMALLER.

## Context Efficiency

Every token spent *finding* code is a token not spent *reasoning* about code.
- Prefer targeted lookups (grep for specific symbols, read specific functions) over broad file reads.
- When exploring, read only the relevant section of a file, not the entire file.
- If you already found what you need, stop searching.
- Avoid re-reading files you've already read in this session.

## Verification

Reuse the inherited cache for ordinary uv commands.
Preserve any explicit `UV_CACHE_DIR`; that path remains caller-owned.
Use the contributor guide's private-cache recipe when isolation is required.
Never directly prune a shared uv cache.

Before committing, ALWAYS run:
- Targeted tests: the tests covering the files your change touches, and the tests you added.
- Static gates on the files you touched: lint and format, the type checker and the complexity gate (ruff, mypy and xenon in a Python repo).
- If you changed frontend files: the frontend tests for those files, and the browser checks for just the surfaces you touched — `npm run ui-check -- <module> ...`, naming the `frontend/scripts/ui-checks/` modules for those surfaces. Never a bare `npm run ui-check` in this container: the merge verify runs every browser check whenever `frontend/` changed. A scoped run fails when there is no Chromium; if it does, report the browser checks as not run, never as passed.
- The configured verify command, `make test`, only when it is a scoped check: read it first, and skip it when it runs the whole test suite, semgrep or the docs checks (a script that mirrors CI does). Say in your report which you did.
- Do NOT run the full test suite, semgrep or the docs checks in this container: together they exceed its 8 GB memory cap, the run is OOM-killed and your work is lost. The merge verify runs the full suite and semgrep on the verify host; that is not this run's job.

**Execution rule:** Never end your turn waiting on a background task or
notification — run every gate in the foreground, or poll it synchronously to
completion. The run finalizes at end-of-turn, so anything left in the

## Pre-Publish Self-Check

Your last step, and ONE bounded pass: no loop, no second opinion, and no
substitute for a review round — the adversarial review still runs after you.

Read your own change the way that reviewer will read it, pinned to the merge
base:

```
git diff origin/main...HEAD
```

That three-dot diff IS the change under review. A diff of the working tree
alone shows only what you have not committed yet, so it is not what the
reviewer sees; if `origin/main` is absent here, this checkout has no `origin`
remote and the bare branch name is the base.

Check that diff against the rubric below, fix what fails, then re-run the
verification commands above. Then stop: do NOT write a judgement, a findings
list, or any machine-readable result file. Recording findings is the review
stage's job, and a judgement of your own is not an input to it.

### The reviewer's own checklist

Quoted from the pinned reviewer rubric (sha b178fcd3e528) — the rubric this diff will
actually be reviewed against, with its judgement and reporting contract
removed, because none of that is yours to produce:

### What to do

1. Read the PR diff, and the recorded acceptance criteria the dispatch
   environment states below it under "Acceptance criteria (host-recorded
   plan)". Those criteria are what the item asked for; kew read them out of the
   issue and recorded them before the implementation ran. Judge the diff
   against them AND against everything below. If the dispatch states no
   criteria section, the item has none recorded and you judge the diff alone.
2. Look specifically for interactions with actors OUTSIDE the implementing
   session's context — a concurrent driver, a live claim, a reconcile/repair
   loop, the next cooldown tick, a second copy of the same process. Same-context
   self-review cannot see these; that is why you exist.
3. Where you assert a defect, EXECUTE evidence for it: run the command that
   demonstrates it and capture the output. A claim without executed evidence is
   not admissible and will be dropped.

### A green result is not self-validating

Step 3 above requires executed evidence. This section is about the evidence
itself: a passing test, a red mutation, and a deleted function can each mean
something other than what they appear to. Every pattern below was found in this
repository, each after a change had already been reviewed and believed correct.

- **A check its own harness repairs.** The condition the check looks for is
  silently fixed before the assertion runs. Seen three times in one day: a probe
  fixture neither version would ever flag; a dry run that could not exercise the
  code path because the ids it needed are only populated on create; a lockfile
  assertion that the test runner re-locked before reading. Ask: *what would have
  to be true for this to fail?* If you cannot name it, it is not a check.
- **An assertion on the wrong channel.** A test asserted a hook did not run by
  searching captured stdout; hook output does not reliably land there, so it
  passed against the vulnerable code too. Prefer asserting an *effect* — a file,
  a row, a returned value — over a string in an output stream.
- **A red result that is not a failure.** A mutation that produces collection
  ERRORS rather than assertion failures proves nothing about what the test
  checks; it only proves the module stopped importing. Confirm the failure is
  the assertion you meant to trip.
- **A passing test that stopped testing.** Adding a decorator above an existing
  `@patch` shifts positional mock injection, so a fixture parameter silently
  receives a mock. The test still passes while configuring a `MagicMock` repr as
  its input. Check that added patches, fixtures, and parameters still line up.
- **A complete-looking set of checks with a gap.** A claim was verified three
  ways — directory, config, hooks — and was still false, because the object
  store was never checked. For a negative claim ("X cannot reach Y"), enumerate
  what Y *is* — every resource, not the accesses someone thought of.
- **A correct deletion that removes a guarantee.** Deleting a mechanism can be
  right while the guarantee it provided still matters somewhere else. The tests
  encoding that guarantee are often deleted in the same diff, so nothing goes
  red. When a diff removes protective code, ask what it protected and where that
  protection lives now.

### Test changes

A PR passes every gate by running its own tests, so a PR that weakens those
tests passes them. Check the diff's test changes for each of these patterns:

- **removed or loosened asserts** — an `assert` deleted, or narrowed to
  something weaker (`is not None`, `in`, a truthiness check);
- **deleted tests** — a `test_*` function or test file gone;
- **added skip/xfail** — `pytest.mark.skip`, `skipif`, `xfail`,
  `pytest.skip(...)`, `unittest.skip`;
- **changed expected values** — the literal an assert compares against edited
  to match new output;
- **test-only fix rounds** — a commit after the first that touches tests and no
  production code, i.e. the fix was to the test;
- **`mock.ANY`** — an argument check replaced with a wildcard;
- **broadened `pytest.raises`** — a `match=` dropped, or the expected type
  widened to `Exception`/`BaseException`;
- **production code that detects a test run** — `PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST`,
  `"pytest" in sys.modules`, or any branch that behaves differently under test.

- `ACCEPTED` with a `reason` naming the issue line or the PR's **Behavior
  changes** line that justifies the change;

When the defect is only that a justified test change is not declared — a
REJECTED flag for an edited test no line declares, or for a removed test, that
a **Behavior changes** line in the PR body would settle — file that finding with
`"kind": "declaration"` and `"node_ids"`: the exact pytest node ids to declare,
and only those your evidence shows the head's tests no longer meet. kew then
asks the remediation for those lines and no code change. Every other defect —
including one in the same test file, or a test change no line could justify —
is an ordinary finding with no `kind`. Never put both in one finding.

## Container Environment

You are running inside the sandbox image. `uv`, `git`, `node`/`npm`, and `ps`
(procps) are preinstalled and on PATH — run `uv run pytest` and `npm test`
directly; do NOT re-download uv or install tooling into `/work` (it litters the
checkout you must not commit). Your HOME tmpfs is `exec`, so anything you do
install lands there, not in the bind-mounted checkout.

The container has a hard process/thread cap (`--pids-limit 1024`). Stop any
dev server you started before you run `npm run ui-check` — ui-check starts its
own. In this container, run it only in its scoped form,
`npm run ui-check -- <module> ...`.

`gh` is **deliberately absent** — the container holds no GitHub token by design.
Do not try to install it. Skip any `gh`-dependent tests and say so, per-gate, in
your Dispatch Report. Likewise note any offline-only gate (semgrep, pip-audit,
gitleaks, frontend gates that need network) you could not run.
